newsitem.title: USA: New family finance magazine for boomers.
newsitem.headline: New family finance magazine for boomers.

text.p: Nine out of 10 Baby Boomers do not read personal finance magazines. Citing this statistic, Family Money, a new magazine from the publishers of Better Homes and Gardens, wants to change all that.
"Our readers are primarily concerned with how to finance their kids' educations and how to save enough for retirement," said editor Charley Blaine.

To be published quarterly, Family Money looks at issues that affect adults and families, not just serious investors. Articles in the first issue discuss buying a computer, buying a car vs. leasing one, remarriage and money and collecting for fun and profit.
One article on investment clubs says that over 1,000 new clubs are formed each month and the successful ones build profits, knowlege and a social network.

Family Money also came up with 10 mutual funds that it considers to be the most family-friendly, and will update the list quarterly. The current funds include some administered by Vanguard, Fidelity and Neuberger and Berman.
In the article, "Teach your children how to be smart consumers," the author advises that parents be a role model.

"Show your children how to read labels for nutritional information, check for good workmanship when you buy clothes, and consider more than just styling and color when you purchase a car, an appliance or a piece of furniture."
The magazine, which is available on newsstands, has an introductory cover price of $2.95. All future editions will cost $3.50.
For information on a yearly subscription ($14) or newsstand availability, call the Family Money subscription office at 1-800-642-9607.
Skagen, the Danish-inspired line of watches and sunglasses, plans to come out with clothing for men and women by year 2000.
Designed with "a Danish sensibility," the clothes will be simple, classic styles, said Charlotte Jorst, co-president and co-founder of the company with her husband, Henrik.
She said the women's clothes, particularly, will be designed to fit women of all sizes, not just the tall and thin.
The Jorsts, natives of Denmark, settled in Incline Village, Nev., by Lake Tahoe, where they established Skagen.
The company's watches, which generally sell for under $100, are available in major department stores.
Sunglasses, which were recently introduced, sell for about $50.
For more information on Skagen's clothing line, contact the company at 1-800-937-3576.
Sometimes it's what's on the bag that counts more than what's in the bag. Designer shopping bags are an art form in themselves.
From Bloomingdale's to Armani AX to Starbucks, shopping bags are some of our culture's most powerful advertising tools.
A new book, "Graphis Shopping Bag I," is a collection of 200 of the world's most beautiful shopping bags.
Published by Graphis Books and co-sponsored by the retail trade group, National Retail Federation, the book sells for $69.95.
Published in August, the book is available in some book stores or can be ordered by calling 1-800-209-4234.

The Baby School Co. Inc. says it is never too early to let children watch videos. "So Smart!," a video designed for infants ages 3 months through 1-1/2 years, "assists the development of new neural/brain connections by helping babies identify objects in the real world; attend to new information; assimilate and orient to new and more complex stimuli" and other activities, the company said.
"So Smart!" is 30 minutes long, divided into six five-minute segments. It is intended to be watched in short increments of 10-15 minutes or less.
Parents can interact with their baby during the video by naming objects as they appear, touching and communicating with their babies, the company said in a statement.
The video costs $14.95, plus $3.95 for shipping and handling. It is available immediately through the 800 number but will be in stores in late September.
The Baby School Co. is based in Miami Beach, Fla. For more information on the video, call 1-800-663-2741.
